content.title: Relationship Between Sample Size and Margin of Error
content.overview: In statistics, there is an inverse relationship between sample size and margin of error. Understanding this relationship is crucial for evaluating the precision of statistical inferences.
learning_objectives: Understand the effect of sample size ($n$) on the magnitude of the margin of error.
Identify how increasing the sample size improves the precision of an estimate while keeping the confidence level constant.
Master how to predict trends in the margin of error based on changes in sample size for the SAT.

sections.title: Core Concept: Inverse Relationship
sections.content:
The margin of error reflects the potential difference between a sample statistic and the true population parameter. Sample size refers to the number of individuals included in a study. When other conditions (such as confidence level and data variability) remain constant, a larger sample size results in a smaller margin of error. This means a larger sample provides a more precise estimate.

![Sample Size vs. Margin of Error](https://img.justsolvely.com/followUpImage/3bdba866-b03b-46fb-877d-7d12fc9f0e5f-1786502349961-720.webp)

sections.title: Why Sample Size Affects Error
sections.content: Intuitively, if you randomly survey more people from a large population, your results will be more representative of the entire group. Mathematically, the margin of error is generally inversely proportional to the square root of the sample size $n$. Therefore, while increasing the sample size reduces the error, the rate of decrease slows down as $n$ increases.

sections.title: Practical Application of Sample Size Changes
sections.content: On the SAT, you will often encounter scenarios comparing two studies. If Study A has a sample size of 100 and Study B has a sample size of 400 (assuming the same sampling method and confidence level), then Study B's margin of error will be smaller than Study A's. Specifically, if the sample size increases by 4 times, the margin of error is typically halved.

worked_examples.question: A research institute surveyed 200 randomly selected residents and found that 60% supported the construction of a new park, with a margin of error of 5%. If the institute conducts a second survey of 800 randomly selected residents using the same sampling method and the confidence level remains the same, what is the most likely margin of error for the second survey?
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Compare sample sizes. The sample size of the second survey (800) is 4 times that of the first survey (200). Step 2: Apply the inverse relationship principle. As sample size increases, the margin of error decreases. Step 3: Quantitative estimation. The margin of error is inversely proportional to the square root of the sample size. Since the sample size becomes 4 times the original, the margin of error becomes $1/\sqrt{4} = 1/2$ of the original. Step 4: Calculate the result. $5\% * 0.5 = 2.5\%$. Therefore, the margin of error for the second survey is approximately 2.5%.

common_mistakes: Incorrectly assuming that sample size is directly proportional to the margin of error (i.e., larger sample size means larger error).
Thinking that doubling the sample size will halve the margin of error (it is actually related to the square root; doubling does not result in halving).
Ignoring prerequisite conditions, such as the requirement that sampling must be random and the confidence level must remain consistent.
exam_tips: On the SAT, if a question asks how to reduce the margin of error, the preferred answer is usually 'increase the sample size'.
Remember the core mantra: 'Larger Sample = Smaller Error'.
Pay attention to whether the question mentions 'random sampling'; if the sampling is not random, increasing the sample size may not yield a reliable margin of error.
content.recap: There is a clear inverse relationship between sample size and margin of error: provided the confidence level is consistent, increasing the sample size will narrow the margin of error, making statistical inferences more precise.

knowledge_claims.content: All other factors being equal, sample size and margin of error have an inverse relationship.
Increasing the sample size typically leads to a decrease in the margin of error.
Decreasing the sample size typically leads to an increase in the margin of error.
The size of the margin of error is inversely proportional to the square root of the sample size $n$.
To halve the margin of error, the sample size must be increased to 4 times its original size, assuming other factors remain constant.
A larger sample size means the sample statistic provides a more precise estimate of the population parameter.
When comparing the margins of error of two studies, it must be ensured that their confidence levels are the same.
It is incorrect to believe that doubling the sample size will reduce the margin of error by half.
It is incorrect to believe that a larger sample size results in a larger margin of error.
When evaluating the reliability of a statistical study, one should check if the sample size is large enough to maintain a small margin of error.
